title: Reserve Asset Competition and the Global Fiscal Cycle

p.t: In the past two decades, governments around the world embarked on fiscal expansions. As shown in Figure (1), developed countries' government debt increased dramatically during the 2008 financial crisis, and then again during the COVID-19 recession. A substantial amount of the variation in government debt/GDP ratios across countries can be explained by a single common factor, which we refer to as the global fiscal cycle. This global fiscal cycle has important implications for our understanding of developed countries' fiscal sustainability, as well as for shaping the global demand for government liabilities as reserve assets. There are a number of potential explanations for the existence of the global fiscal cycle. First, demand for reserve assets tends to increase during global flight-to-safety episodes. This increased demand for reserve assets raises convenience yields on government debt and incentivizes government issuers to take advantage of the favorable funding terms. Second, countries have correlated business cycles. When they all enter recessions, the marginal benefits of expansionary fiscal policies tend to rise relative to the fiscal costs of additional debt issuances. As a result, correlated business cycles could also give rise to correlated debt issuances. Both channels relate the fiscal expansions in recent decades to the global financial crisis and the covid-19 crisis, as these crises could trigger a flight to safety and increase demand for reserve assets on the one hand, and increase the marginal efficacy of government spending on the other.

In this paper, we propose a third, novel explanation: the global fiscal cycle can arise when governments compete in the provision of reserve assets. By modeling the behavior of the governments in a setting in which reserve assets are imperfect substitutes, we show that a form of strategic complementarity leads other governments to issue more debt when one government issues more debt. As a result, a fiscal shock local to one country could trigger a global response in debt issuance, even when their demand and supply factors are uncorrelated. We begin the paper by presenting empirical evidence on the global fiscal cycle. We first document the existence of a large common component in the growth of global debt/GDP ratios: the first principal component of the growth in debt/GDP ratios explains over 50% of their variation. Interestingly, a substantial fraction of the variation in debt/GDP growth in our panel remains unex-plained by global business cycle variables. This unexplained variation points toward an additional channel which drives the global fiscal cycle. Then, as evidence for the channel we propose in this paper, we present two sets of empirical tests on the response of government debt issuances to other countries' government debt issuances. First, we extract idiosyncratic shocks to U.S. debt issuance that are unexplained by the business cycle variables, and show that these shocks explain a substantial amount of debt issuance in other countries. Second, we construct an instrument for U.S. debt issuances using the narrative approach developed by Romer and Romer (2010). Specifically, we extend their methodology to identify exogenous tax changes from 1980 to 2023, focusing on policy changes motivated by long-run growth considerations. Using this instrument, we demonstrate that exogenous increases in U.S.

debt issuance lead to significant increases in foreign countries' debt issuances. Both empirical tests suggest that a 10% increase in instrumented U.S. debt/GDP growth generates around a 2-7% increase in debt/GDP growth for the average non-U.S. developed country. These findings provide strong evidence for the existence of strategic complementarity in debt issuance across countries, even when controlling for global business cycle factors. Motivated by our empirical findings, we develop a model of demand and supply for reserve assets. This model generates a novel strategic complementarity in the issuance of reserve assets. We present the results in three steps. We first consider the benchmark in which all governments are infinitesimally small. On the demand side, a representative investor derives utility from earning returns and from directly holding the reserve assets. The reserve assets are imperfect substitutes and are aggregated by a constant elasticity of substitution (CES) function with country-specific weights. As a result, reserve assets earn varying degrees of convenience yields, which are decreasing in their quantities outstanding and also depend on how much the investor values them for their reserve status. On the supply side, each government balances the trade-off in debt issuance between earning the seigniorage revenues due to the convenience yields and incurring fiscal costs from debt repayment. We model the fiscal costs in a reduced form as an increasing function of the quantity of debt issued. On the one hand, the government prefers higher seigniorage revenues since they could be used to fund domestic households' consumption. This term reflects the profit maximization view of government debt issuance as in Farhi and Maggiori (2018); Brunnermeier, Merkel, and Sannikov (2022). On the other hand, debt has to be paid back in the future, and the marginal utility of government spending declines with each additional dollar of spending. In equilibrium, we show that each government issuer charges a constant and proportional markup above its marginal cost of issuance. In particular, the equilibrium markup, conditional on the government's own issuance, does not depend on other governments' actions.

In our second step, we assume the governments are "granular": there are a finite number of governments and they have non-zero mass. In this case, the equilibrium markup each government charges on its debt is no longer a constant fraction of the marginal cost. Instead, the markup is adjusted by a factor related to the market share of each government's debt. Intuitively, when an asset has a higher market share, it faces a more inelastic demand curve because there are fewer assets to substitute towards. As a result, each government takes the market impact of its debt issuance decision into account and responds to other governments' issuances. Similar to standard results in oligopoly, when the demand curve becomes more inelastic, each government wants to under-supply relative to the competitive benchmark and raise its markup. To understand the economics of the granular case, suppose one government (say, the U.S.) decides to issue more debt for idiosyncratic reasons. For other governments, this means their market shares decline and they earn lower seigniorage revenues, which leads to two considerations. First, the increase in debt issuance in the U.S. increases the global supply of reserve assets. Given the reserve assets are imperfect substitutes and the representative investor has a downward-sloping demand curve, the marginal seigniorage revenue that other government issuers can collect goes down. As a result, holding the supply curve fixed, other issuers will issue less debt because it has become less profitable to do so.

Second, each issuer's supply curve depends on its market share. When the U.S. issues more debt, other issuers' market shares decline, which means that they face a more elastic demand curve and are incentivized to issue more debt. This feature gives rise to a strategic complementarity in debt issuance, so that other issuers' supply curves rotate in response to the U.S. issuance and motivates them to issue more debt and regain market shares. In our parameterization, when the governments are granular, the second consideration dominates, implying that other governments will issue more debt when a government issues more. In stark contrast, when the governments are infinitesimally small, only the first consideration is operative, as their market shares are effectively zero. In this case, governments will issue less debt when a non-zero mass of foreign governments issue more. In the last step, we conduct a decomposition to answer how much of the global fiscal cycle is driven by common demand and supply shocks and by strategic complementarity identified in this paper. We take a stance on the preference parameters based on the prior literature that exploits exogenous variation for identification. Then, we estimate the model using method of moments, as we can back out each government's marginal cost of debt issuance and its convenience weight in the investor's preference based on the observed convenience yields and debt quantities. This estimated model allows us to understand the effect of the reserve asset competition. We find that, once we turn off the strategic complementarity by assuming all governments behave as infinitesimally small issuers, the commonality in the fiscal cycles as measured by the variance explained by the first principal component declines from 70% to below 40% in the post-1998 sample which we use in our model estiamtion. This result suggests that correlated fundamentals and our novel reserve asset competition channel each explain about half of the commonality in the global fiscal cycle.

Our estimated model also allows us to revisit the notion of U.S. specialness in the global financial system. We find that the U.S. and the U.K. have the highest convenience weights among all countries in our sample, whereas Switzerland has the lowest. Importantly, our analysis reveals that a country's convenience weight does not necessarily correspond directly to its observed convenience yield. For instance, while Germany has a higher convenience yield than France, it issues much less debt. As a result, we back out similar levels of convenience weights for these two coun-tries. This nuanced perspective on the "exorbitant privilege" suggests that the U.S.'s dominance in the reserve asset market manifests not only through higher convenience yields but also through its capacity to issue larger quantities of debt. Our findings thus provide a new quantitative framework for understanding the multifaceted nature of the U.S.'s special status in global financial markets. Literature Review. Our paper contributes to a recent literature that studies governments' capacity to issue reserve assets and raise seigniorage revenues (Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen, 2012;He, Krishnamurthy, Milbradt, et al., 2015;Farhi and Maggiori, 2018;Bahaj and Reis, 2020;Clayton, Dos Santos, Maggiori, and Schreger, 2022;Coppola, Krishnamurthy, and Xu, 2023). In particular, Brunnermeier, Merkel, andSannikov (2020, 2022) raise the concept of the "government Laffer curve", which describes the trade-off between the amount of debt issued and the seigniorage revenue from debt issuance. Our paper studies the strategic interaction between multiple sovereign issuers when their incentives to issue debt vary across business cycles. Our paper is also related to the literature that examines fiscal sustainability through the lens of the government budget constraint (Jiang, Lustig, Van Nieuwerburgh, andXiaolan, 2019, 2021;Jiang, 2021Jiang, , 2022;;Mian, Straub, and Sufi, 2022). Croce, Kung, Nguyen, and Schmid (2012) study how fiscal policy affects asset prices in a general equilibrium model. We highlight a novel strategic driver of the common variation in fiscal dynamics.

On the empirical side, Krishnamurthy and Li (2020); Choi, Kirpalani, and Perez (2022) exploit exogenous variation to identify investors' demand elasticities for reserve assets. Koijen and Yogo (2020); Jiang, Richmond, and Zhang (2022); Fang, Hardy, and Lewis (2022) also study their substitution patterns using demand system models. Gomez Cram, Kung, and Lustig (2023) study how the Treasury's yield and convenience yield are affected by fiscal policy news. Our empirical part builds on these works, and explores the substitution patterns between different sovereign issuers' reserve assets. To do so, we construct an instrument for U.S. debt issuances using the Romer and Romer (2010) narrative approach and show that this instrument can explain foreign debt issuances. Our result also generates a novel micro-foundation for the impact of granularity in international economics. Granularity refers to the notion that idiosyncratic movements from large economic agents do not average out in aggregate, and could in fact cause spill-over effects to others (Gabaix, 2011). In our paper, we show that "granular effects" arise in the fiscal context due to strategic interactions of governments.

This section documents a number of empirical facts about the global fiscal cycle and its relation to other global factors, such as those that drive the global business cycle. Building on these facts, the next section proposes a novel explanation for the existence of the global fiscal cycle.

We obtain data on economic quantities from Oxford Economics. These data series include the quantity of outstanding general government debt, GDP, price level indices, interest rates, and unemployment rates. In this section we use the U.S. 1-year Treasury yield from Global Financial Data and construct foreign interest rates as the U.S. Treasury yield plus the 1-year forward premium, which is based on the exchange rate and currency forward rate data from Datastream. Our panel covers 8 developed countries which we consider as potential reserve asset issuers: Canada, France, Germany, Japan, Netherlands, Switzerland, United Kingdom, and the United States. Our sample is quarterly and runs from 1980Q1 to 2023Q4. Appendix A contains more details on the data construction.

p.s: Common Factors in Global Fiscal Policy
p.t: We begin by documenting the existence of a global fiscal cycle in countries' government debt issuances, building on Jiang (2022). We calculate the year-on-year log growth in the government debt quantity in each country, and conduct a principal component analysis. Figure (2) reports a striking result: the first principal component (PC1) captures about 52% of the variation. All coun-tries have positive loadings on PC1, although there is considerable heterogeneity in the magnitude of the loadings. In other words, when countries choose to issue more debt, they tend to do so at the same time. This first principal component is strongly correlated with the simple equal-weighted average of debt growth with a correlation of 0.99. As a result, in the next exercise, we use this equal-weighted average of countries' log debt growth as our measure of the global fiscal cycle.

Given that there is a common factor in different countries' debt issuances, a natural question is whether this common factor is related to other standard business cycle measures. We now show that while there is some relation between the global fiscal cycle and common business cycle factors, the global fiscal cycle also has a substantial component unexplained by business cycle variables. In Table (1), we regress the average log increase in debt/GDP ratio on the average log changes in GDP, CPI, interest rates, and unemployment rates. Each of these series themselves contain a large common component. For example, the first principal component of log GDP growth also explains 72% of the variation in GDP growth. Columns (1) to (3) show that the common variations in inflation and interest rate changes individually explain a maximum of 19% of the variation in the average debt growth, while the common variation in GDP growth is not correlated with average debt growth. Column (4) shows that the common variation in unemployment growth has a stronger explanatory power, which suggests that fiscal policies in these countries are related to the unemployment cycle. Column (5) includes all 4 variables together and shows these standard business cycle explain 57% of the variation in the global fiscal cycle, which leaves about half of the variation in the fiscal cycle unexplained. This result suggests that while a portion of the global fiscal cycle is related to factors representing the global business cycle, a large component of the global fiscal cycle is orthogonal to these factors.

p.s: Foreign Responses to Idiosyncratic Debt Expansions
p.t: Our results so far document the extent to which different countries' debt/GDP ratios comove. These comovements can come from either correlated macroeconomic fundamentals that lead these countries to make correlated borrowing decisions, or strategic responses to each other's debt issuance. To distinguish between these two possibilities, we next examine whether an exogenous event in a country that leads to its own debt expansion also drives debt expansion in other countries. We consider two approaches. First, in this section, we extract idiosyncratic U.S. shocks using a statistical model of the drivers of U.S. issuance decisions and show that these shocks can explain foreign issuances. Second, in the next section, we construct an instrument for U.S. issuances and show that instrumented U.S. debt issuances can explain foreign debt issuances. We begin with our first approach of using a statistical model to extract idiosyncratic U.S. debt issuances. Our null hypothesis is that the change in U.S. government debt issuance is driven by policy responses to its own business cycles and idiosyncratic shocks which are orthogonal to the business cycles of other countries. Similarly, foreign government debt issuances are driven by their own business cycles and idiosyncratic shocks. As a result, while U.S. government debt issuance can be correlated with foreign debt issuances because the U.S. business cycle is correlated with foreign business cycles, the idiosyncratic component of U.S. debt issuance should be orthogonal to foreign debt issuances. If we observe that this idiosyncratic component is in fact correlated with foreign debt issuances, then, we can reject the null and find support for the view that the foreign debt issuances in fact respond to the idiosyncratic component in the U.S. debt issuance.

p.s: Foreign Responses to Idiosyncratic Debt Expansions
p.t: We extract the idiosyncratic component in U.S. debt issuance by regressing the year-on-year change in the U.S. debt/GDP ratio on the U.S. business cycle variables x U S,t , which include U.S. GDP growth, inflation, change in interest rate, and unemployment growth: and collecting the residual u U S,t as the idiosyncratic component. Then, we regress the year-on-year change in the debt/GDP ratio in each foreign country i on the U.S. idiosyncratic component: where we control for country-level fixed effects α i and the business cycle variables x i,t in the foreign country. Table ( 2) reports this regression with and without the foreign business cycle variables as controls. Both columns suggest that the U.S. idiosyncratic component has a positive and significant effect on the foreign debt expansions. In terms of magnitudes, the first column implies that a 10% increase in idiosyncratic debt/GDP growth leads to a 2% to 4.5% increase in debt/GDP growth for foreign countries -a non-trivial response.

p.s: Foreign Responses to Exogenous Tax Changes
p.t: Next, we turn to our second approach of empricially demonstrating the reserve asset competition channel. In particular, we construct an instrument for U.S. debt issuances that is plausibly uncorrelated with foreign countries' business cycle conditions and government debt issuance decisions. To do so, we extend Romer and Romer (2010)'s narrative approach to identify tax shocks from 1980 to 2023. Appendix B contains the full details of how we extend their approach to our full sample. Romer and Romer (2010) use narrative records such as presidential speeches, executive-branch documents, and Congressional reports to categorize fiscal shocks into four groups: (1) endogenous countercyclical policies to return growth to normal, (2) endogenous policies motivated by spending changes, (3) exogenous policies to deal with an inherited budget deficit, and (4) exogenous policies motivated by a desire to raise long-run growth. For our purposes, we are interested in shocks to U.S. fiscal policy that are driven by decisions that are unrelated to global macroeconomic conditions or other countries' issuance decisions. Given this, we only use the shocks from category (4), which we believe are the most likely to satisfy our exclusion restriction. As Romer and Romer (2010) notes, a very common reason for tax cut under this category is one in which policymakers say that the economy is doing fine (output is growing normally), but they want output to grow faster than normal. This category also includes tax cuts for philosophical reasons, such as to shrink the size of government or for fairness.

p.s: Foreign Responses to Exogenous Tax Changes
p.t: Before turning to our main tests, we document two important features of the data on these tax policy shocks and government debt issuances. First, it takes time for changes in tax policy to affect government borrowing. In Figure (3), we compute local projections by regressing the cumulative sum of debt growth rates from period t onward on the "long-run growth" category of tax change in period t. This figure shows that the debt growth rate declines steadily in the following 8 quarters after the tax change, and then slowly reverts to the pre-change level. Given this, we aggregate the tax changes over 2-year rolling windows up to period t and denote this variable as RR U S,t , which captures the exogenous tax changes in the U.S. that lead to its own debt reduction. Second, U.S. government debt growth has a very different distribution before and after 2008. In Figure (4), we report the histogram of the realized year-on-year debt growth rates in the U.S. and color them by the pre-and post-2008 periods. We observe that the distribution of debt growth rates is more dispersed after 2008, and the mean debt growth rate is much higher (0.7% vs. 2.8% yearon-year). Given this regime break, debt growth that appears to be much higher than the average in the pre-2008 period may not be as high in the post-2008 period. As a result, we control for the differences in debt growth rates separately before and after 2008 by including a dummy variable

p.s: Foreign Responses to Exogenous Tax Changes
p.t: With these observations in hand, we empirically demonstrate the existence of the reserve asset competition change by regressing the year-on-year U.S. and foreign debt growth on the 8-quarter tax change RR U S,t : We report the results in Table (3). In column (1), we find that a higher tax increase, which lowers the need for government borrowing, indeed leads to a lower debt issuance in the U.S. Moreover, as shown in column (2), this exogenous tax change also leads to a lower debt issuance in foreign countries, and the point estimates are similar between the U.S. and foreign countries. So, consistent with our previous result using the idiosyncratic U.S. debt expansions, we find that an exogenous event in the U.S. that leads to its own debt expansion also drives debt expansion in other countries of similar magnitudes.

p.s: A Model of Reserve Asset Competition
p.t: In this section, we present our model of reserve asset competition. We begin with the presentation of the demand side and then present the supply side.

We consider government debt in a finite number of advanced economies as reserve assets. We index these countries by n ∈ {1, . . . , N }. The government in country n issues a reserve asset of a unique variety. Let r t (n) denote its yield, and let µ t denote the competitive funding rate. Then, r t (n) -µ t denotes the excess return of the asset, which is possibly negative due to the desirability of the reserve asset. We refer to µ t -r t (n) as the convenience yield. There is a representative investor who can invest in all countries' reserve assets and takes prices as given. 1 This investor maximizes their utility, which is a combination of the excess returns earned on these assets and the additional liquidity benefit that depends on a constant elasticity of substitution (CES) aggregate over the N reserve assets: 1 Alternatively, we can consider a unit mass of infinitesimally small and competitive investors and obtain the same results. where q t (n) denotes the quantity of the safe asset from country n that is held by this investor. The CES aggregator is a multi-asset generalization of the money demand in Poterba and Rotemberg (1986); Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen (2012); Nagel (2016). The coefficient λ t captures the representative investor's overall demand for reserve assets, which we refer to as the convenience demand parameter. We also introduce heterogeneous weights ω t (n) in the CES aggregation, which we refer to as the convenience weight of safe asset n. This weight measures the importance of this asset in terms of fulfilling the investor's demand for liquidity and safety. We assume ω t (n) ≥ 0 for all reserve assets n, and we normalize the convenience weights by

We assume the investor has deep pockets and faces a competitive funding cost, µ t . If there is an asset m without convenience benefit (i.e., ω t (m) = 0), then the first-order condition becomes r t (m) = µ t . So, the funding cost µ t can also be interpreted as the risk-free rate without the convenience yield. Otherwise, the first-order condition w.r.t. q t (n) implies which demonstrates that the coefficient ρ governs the elasticity of the substitution between reserve assets issued by different countries. We use Q t to denote an index of the aggregate quantity of liquidity provided by all the reserve assets: Then, we have the following result that characterizes the demand for reserve asset n: Lemma 1. Given ρ < 1, the demand for reserve asset n is decreasing in the convenience yield µ t -r t (n) and increasing in the convenience weight ω t (n): ( Lemma 1 implies the following equilibrium relationship: On the left-hand side, Q t is the index of the aggregate liquidity provided by all the reserve assets, which directly enters the investor's utility. On the right-hand side, N k=1 (µ t -r t (k))q t (k) is the total amount of pecuniary payoff that the investor gives up in order to hold these reserve assets.

This term on the right-hand side also captures the total amount of the seigniorage revenue earned by all reserve issuers combined. As a result, the coefficient θ governs the elasticity of substitution between earning higher returns and obtaining higher liquidity benefits. If θ > 1, then, a lower provision of the aggregate liquidity is associated with a higher amount of the seigniorage revenue. This simple demand specification provides a reason why the observed convenience yields, , do not directly map to the convenience weights, ω t (n). For example, consider U.S. and Swiss government debt. Even when the observed convenience yield µ t -r t (n) is the same for the two assets, it is still possible for the U.S. debt to have a much higher convenience weight, ω t (U S), which would then manifest itself as a much greater quantity outstanding of the U.S. safe assets, q t (U S). In other words, depending on how much debt is issued, the "exorbitant privilege" of the U.S. government can show up either in the quantity of debt issued, or in the convenience yield. This result requires that the assets are less-than-perfect substitutes, i.e., ρ < 1. If all reserve assets are perfect substitutes (i.e., ρ → 1), the convenience weight ω t (n) is fully manifested in the observed convenience yield µ t -r t (n). In this case, the quantities are determined by market clearing, and the convenience yields satisfy

Finally, while our demand side specification uses the standard CES aggregator, 0 < ρ < 1 is not a sufficient condition for the reserve assets being substitutes. We deviate from the textbook consumer problem with CES aggregation over goods in two ways: first, in our setting, the reserve assets also have pecuniary payoff in addition to the convenience utility derived from the CES function; second, investors have access to an elastic supply of funds at the competitive funding rate, as opposed to a fixed budget. In Appendix C.2, we provide a detailed discussion of these two features, and show that the reserve assets are imperfect substitutes only if 0 < ρ < 1 and θ > 1-ρ, which is the parameter region we consider in the paper. Having said that, even though the reserve assets are imperfect substitutes in partial equilibrium, strategic interaction between the issuers will lead to a complementarity in their debt issuance decisions and give rise to global comovements in issuance decisions, as we show next.

We now turn to the supply side, which contains N government issuers. We assume that each government faces the same competitive discount rate µ t , and its utility from debt issuance is where the first term represents the seigniorage revenue from issuing debt at a yield below the competitive discount rate, and the second term represents the fiscal cost of debt issuance. The fiscal cost can be interpreted as the cost of future taxation that is required to pay back the debt, minus the benefit of government spending that is made possible in the current period. This term could potentially capture the incentive to save some dry powder for future crisis, or a debt overhang problem, although these considerations are beyond the scope of our model. We assume that the marginal fiscal cost is positive, i.e., C ′ n (q) > 0, since a higher borrowing today implies higher government spending today and higher expected tax in the future. We expect the marginal cost of future taxation to be increasing, while the marginal benefit of current spending to be decreasing. Each government sets the quantity of debt issued to maximize utility, taking other governments' actions as given. Government n's first-order condition is which implies the following rate-setting rule: We interpret µ t as the competitive funding cost, C ′ n (q t (n)) as the marginal cost of debt issuance, and the third term as a markup. Because the governments are oligopolists whose assets are imperfect substitutes, they have incentives to under-supply and charge a price above their marginal cost.

The following proposition characterizes each government issuer's optimal behavior. Proposition 1. Each issuer's optimal markup is a fraction of the marginal issuance cost, which is scaled by a function related to the issuer's market share: (2) To understand this result, we break down this formula into a few steps. First, let us consider the case in which the debt assets issued by all countries are perfect substitutes, i.e., ρ = 1. In this case, The convenience yield is set to be equal to the marginal cost of issuing debt, which is what we expect when the issuers are behaving competitively: Second, we assume that government debt is an imperfect substitute, i.e., ρ < 1. However, the governments are small in the sense that their actions do not affect the aggregate liquidity, which is now an integral over the quantity of debt issued by a unit mass of infinitesimally small governments: In this case, each government's debt issuance is a tiny fraction of the aggregate liquidity, and the optimal markup is a fixed fraction of the marginal issuance cost: This result recovers the standard result under CES aggregation that the optimal markup is a constant fraction of the marginal cost, which we see, for example, in New Keynesian models. A direct implication is that if all governments have identical marginal costs, their bonds should have the same convenience yields. Conversely, if a government's marginal cost is higher, it has a higher convenience yield. This is intuitive: suppose the U.S. has a much higher convenience weight ω t (n)

than Switzerland, and as a result issues much more debt. This puts the U.S. on the far end of the issuance cost curve, thereby incurring a higher marginal cost. In this way, we are able to connect the convenience weight ω t (n) to the convenience yield through the marginal cost function. Finally, when the issuers are big, they take their size into consideration. This effect is captured by the additional term in the denominator on the right-hand side of Eq. ( 2). If an asset has a greater market share, it faces a more inelastic demand curve, because there are fewer assets to substitute with. As a result, this additional effect lowers the denominator below ρ for large issuers, who behave as if they were facing more inelastic demand and therefore charge higher markups. Moreover, this term also depends other issuers' decisions. As we will see in the next subsection, each issuer's optimal issuance strategy now takes other issuers' actions into account.

To further trace out the equilibrium quantities and convenience yields in the small-issuer and bigissuer cases, we consider a numerical example with just two countries, the U.S. (n = 1) and foreign (n = 2). For both countries, we assume that the cost of issuance follows C n (q) = 1 2 γ n q 2 . We assume θ = 1.36 and ρ = 0.7, so that the investors have some curvature in the utility derived from the reserve asset holding, and they perceive the two countries' government bonds as imperfect substitutes. We justify these parameter values in the next section. We consider a symmetric case with λ n = 1, ω = 1, and γ n = 0.1%. This implies bond quantities of q(n) = 4.13 and bond convenience yields of µ t -r t (n) = 5.51%. Now we consider a reduction in the U.S.'s marginal cost of issuing debt. As we discuss above, this can result from the U.S. entering a recession in which the marginal benefit of deficit spending increases. For example, if γ 1 reduces by half. Then, we find a new equilibrium at q(1) = 5.30, q(2) = 4.31, µ t -r t (1) = 4.31%, µ t -r t (2) = 4.87%. In this case, there is strategic complementarity in the two countries' issuance decisions: the foreign country's best response to the fiscal expansion in the U.S. is to also issue more debt, albeit a smaller amount. As a result of higher issuances in both countries, the equilibrium convenience yields decline for both countries' debt and more so for the U.S. because of its higher issuance.

In Figure (6), we plot the equilibrium quantities and convenience yields as functions of the shock to γ 1 . As the U.S. issues more debt due to a reduction in the marginal cost of debt issuance, the foreign country also responds by issuing more debt. The equilibrium convenience yields decline for both countries' debt. To see whether the foreign country's strategic decision play any role in its issuance decision, we next consider the alternative case in which the foreign countries are infinitesimally small. Specifically, we assume that the U.S. accounts for half of the measure of the issuers, whereas an infinite number of foreign countries account for the other half. We again consider a shock to the U.S., and plot the equilibrium quantities and convenience yields as functions of the shock to γ 1 in Figure (7). In this case, consistent with Eq. ( 4), when the issuance cost declines for the U.S., the U.S. issues more debt whereas the foreign countries choose to issue less debt, which is the opposite of the previous case. This numerical result confirms our theoretical result that the strategic interaction between the issuers can lead to a complementarity in their issuance decisions, despite their assets being imperfect substitutes. In the next section, we take this model to the data.

To quantify how the reserve asset competition affects the equilibrium fiscal decisions, we estimate our model using the panel data of reserve assets' quantities and convenience yields. We begin by calibrating the two demand side parameters: the elasticity of substitution between reserve assets, ρ, and the curvature in the utility derived from holding reserve assets, θ. First, for ρ, Krishnamurthy and Li (2022) examine the substitution pattern between bank deposits and Treasury debt, and find the ρ parameter to be between 0.5 and 0.7. This range of the parameter value indicates that bank deposits and Treasury debt are fairly substitutable but are not perfect substitutes. While our focus is the substitution pattern between different government debt, we find this range of elasticity to be plausible. Since the government debt we study in this paper is all on the safer side of the risk spectrum and appears in a basket such as the S&P Global Developed Sovereign Bond Index, we pick 0.7 which is on the higher end of the range. For θ, we link this curvature parameter to the demand elasticity of the reserve assets. Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen (2012) use a long sample to trace out the negative relationship between Treasury supply and bond convenience yield. Quantitatively, they find that a 1% increase in the log U.S. government debt/GDP ratio is associated with a 0.75 basis point decline in the Treasury's convenience yield, which is proxied by the AAA-Treasury yield spread or the commercial paper-Treasury yield spread. Given an average convenience yield of 0.52%, this estimate suggests a demand elasticity of 1%/(0.75/52) = 0.69 approximately.

To interpret this elasticity estimate through the lens of our model, we first note that, in the one-issuer case of our model, the log convenience yield and the log asset quantity satisfy So, the elasticity is equal to which implies that the implied θ parameter is around 1/0.69 = 1.44. With more than one issuer, our equilibrium conditions become , which additionally depends on the share of the U.S. debt in the total liquidity (i.e., ), and how other countries' issuances respond to the convenience yield shock to the U.S. debt (i.e., ). We assume that (1) the U.S. on average accounts for 20% of the total liquidity, which is based on the debt quantity data, the ρ parameter, and the estimated convenience weights ω. We also assume that (2) foreign countries' issuance responses are 72% of the U.S. response, which is based on our empirical estimate using the instrumental variable regressions reported in Table (3). Then, we obtain an implied θ parameter of 1.36, which is close to the single-issuer case. This calibration choice implies that the bond investors have a slight curvature in their utility derived from holding reserve assets.

We estimate our model using the same sample of countries as in the empirical section, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Japan, Netherlands, Switzerland, United Kingdom, and the United States. We use the 1-year Treasury yield to proxy for the debt yield r t (n), and use the 1-year Libor rate to proxy for the competitive funding rate µ t . By using the Treasury-Libor spread as the convenience yield, we implicitly assume that the competitive funding rate can be different across currencies, which is consistent with the evidence presented in the literature on covered interest parity violation (Du et al., 2018). As the Libor rates ceased to be published in recent years, we extend the sample using 1-year swap rates. We obtain a balanced sample for model estimation from 1998Q4 to 2023Q4. Additional details on the data construction are provided in Appendix A. We assume that the observed data are generated by the model with big issuers. We parameterize the marginal cost of issuance as C ′ n (q) = γ t (n)q, where the parameter γ t (n) can be countryspecific and time-varying. We use the market value of outstanding government debt in each country normalized by the concurrent GDP to proxy for the debt quantity q t (n). The normalization by GDP only requires us to rescale the unobserved convenience weights ω t (n) and the issuance costs γ t (n), which does not affect the model's implications.

The unknowns in this model are the unobserved convenience weights ω t (n) and issuance costs γ t (n). We can estimate these parameters using the following equilibrium condition from the supply side, and the following equilibrium condition from the demand side, The number of unknowns matches the number of equilibrium conditions, so that the model is solved exactly. We report the demand side parameter values in Figure (8). The convenience demand λ t increased significantly during the 2008 global financial crisis, and has remained high since then. It had another minor spike in early 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic crisis. On average over our full sample, the U.S. and the U.K. have the highest weights ω t (n). This is consistent with the U.S. being the world's dominant reserve asset. That said, the convenience weight of the U.S. has been declining steadily over the sample. We report the supply side parameter values in Figure (9). The marginal utility of debt issuance, γ t (n), also increased during the 2008 global financial crisis. In the cross-section, Japan has the lowest average issuance cost γ t , which explains why Japan has issued so much debt even after we account for its convenience weight; in comparison, Switzerland and Germany have higher average issuance cost γ t , which explains why they have issued less debt.

p.s: How Much Comovement in Debt Issuances Is Driven by Strategic Interaction?
p.t: Using our estimated model, we can evaluate the role strategic interaction plays in the global comovements in debt issuances. First, taking the U.S. issuance as given, we can ask what each foreign country would have done if it behaved non-strategically. More precisely, we assume that the foreign countries behave like infinitesimally small issuers who do not take the effects of their action into consideration. Instead, they decide their issuance quantities by following the policy specified in Eq. ( 3). We first consider their partial equilibrium response which fixes the behavior of the U.S. and other foreign countries. Table (4) reports the correlation between the log growth rate of the U.S. debt quantity and that of a foreign country's debt quantity. We first report this correlation using the actual quantities of debt issued by each country. Consistent with our earlier empirical results, these countries exhibit a high degree of comovement in their debt issuance. Then, we compute the correlation in the counterfactual case in which the issuers take their marginal cost curves as given but behave like small issuers. The correlation in debt issuance is still positive, which captures the comovements in debt issuance due to the correlated fundamentals. For example, in a recession, the marginal utility of debt issuance goes up for all countries, driving them to issue more debt at the same time. Similarly, if the investor demand for reserve assets goes up, all countries will also respond by issuing more debt.

p.s: How Much Comovement in Debt Issuances Is Driven by Strategic Interaction?
p.t: The difference between the big issuer case and the small issuer case captures the comovements in debt issuance due to strategic interaction. In the last column, we report the fraction of the correlation not captured by the small issuer case. On average, this fraction is 55%, suggesting that strategic interaction among countries plays a quantitatively large role in the global comovements in debt issuance policies. Finally, we consider the general equilibrium responses when all foreign issuers behave nonstrategically. Figure (10) repeats the PCA analysis in the small and big issuer cases. We observe that the first PC explains 73% of the variations in government debt growth across countries in the data, which we assume to coincide with the equilibrium with big issuers. This number drops to around 40% if we take the same parameter value and compute the equilibrium with small issuers. In other words, absent the strategic oligopolist behaviors that arise when issuers are big, the major countries' fiscal cycles demonstrates substantially less commonality.

Our model estimation also helps us revisit the U.S. specialness in the global financial system. As we discussed earlier, each government issuer's convenience weight does not necessarily correspond to its observed convenience yield. More precisely, the demand curve in log can be written as For given aggregate state variables Q t and λ t , each government issuer faces a linear trade-off between the log convenience yield log(µ t -r t (n)) and the log quantity of debt issued log q t (n). If its debt has a higher convenience weight, the demand curve shifts up and the issuer could issue more debt at a given convenience yield. 7). We can see that the pair of the convenience yield and debt quantity implies the U.S. and U.K. have the highest convenience weight, whereas Switzerland has the lowest. A country's convenience weight does not necessarily correspond directly to its observed convenience yield. For instance, while Germany and France lie on the same iso-convenience weight line, Germany has a higher convenience yield than France, whereas France issues more debt. Similarly, while the U.S. debt does not have the highest convenience yield, the sheer quantity of debt issued by the U.S. implies a high convenience weight. This result is consistent with the U.S. specialness in the global financial system, which is driven by the U.S. issuing a large quantity of debt.

In this paper we study competition among countries in the provision of reserve assets and demonstrate how the issuers' strategic interaction can give rise to the global fiscal cycle. Our findings have important implications for understanding the global comovements in government debt issuance, and for the design of optimal fiscal policies in a world where countries are interdependent. Furthermore, our model provides a new perspective on the U.S. specialness in the global financial system, and offers a new way to quantify the convenience weights of different government issuers. p.s: Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT).
p.t: To construct the budget effects of more recent legislation, we extract the list of major federal legislation with significant impacts on revenues from Revenue Projections, by Category, which supplements the Congressional Budget Office (CBO)'s February 2024 report The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2024 to 2034. 2 We then measure the revenue effects of major legislation from the list by referring to documents prepared by the Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT). 3 We download the latest versions of files from the JCT website, detailing the budget or revenue effects of entire legislation or specific revenue provisions covering the period from 2005 to 2027. The comprehensive list of downloaded files is provided in Table A1. The downloaded budget effects of major legislation undergo a data cleaning process that sums the effects of different provisions for each year by each legislation. The basic rules of this process are as follows. We use data available as of the publication date, ignoring future estimates such as "Estimate to be Provided by the Congressional Budget Office." For each piece of legislation, we measure the budget effects for the first five years following the legislation's first year in effect. For each provision under legislation, we consider only the budget effects of the first full year in effect. For instance, if a provision's effective date is 7/1/05, we record the budget effect of 2006, not 2005, as its only budget effect.

p.s: Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT).
p.t: If multiple effective dates are specified for a provision, we generally use the budget effects of the earlier full-cycle year. For example, in the American Recovery And Reinvestment Tax Act Of 2009,foot_2 we use the budget effects of 2010 for Provision II.1. of Title I, when its effective dates are stated for property placed in service after 12/31/09 and 12/31/10. However, if there are multiple effective dates for a provision and one of the dates records no measured effect, we consider only the date with measured effects. For instance, in Division Q of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016, 5 we use the budget effects of 2017 for Provision II.1, as there is no measured effect of this provision in 2016, even though its effective dates are returns and statements relating to calendar years beginning after date of enactment, which is assumed 12/16/15, and credits or refunds made after 12/31/16. If the effective date is unspecified within the document, we assume the first year in effect as the budget effect year. For example, in the American Jobs Creation Act Of 2004, 6 there is no effective date specified for Provision VIII.C.4. 7 Therefore, we assume the budget effect of 2006 as this provision's effect, considering there is no effect measured in 2005, which is the first year available for the entire legislation. If the effective date of a provision is earlier than the first year presented in the table of the legislation's budget effects, we use the first year available in the table as the provision's budget effect. For example, in the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008, 8 we use 2009 as the effective year for Provision III.1., since 2009 is the first year in the table, even though its effective date is sales or exchanges occurring after 12/31/07 in taxable years ending after 12/31/07.

p.s: Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT).
p.t: Several considerations and concerns should be noted regarding the rules stated above. In Division P of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016, 9 multiple provisions record the date of enactment (DOE) as their effective dates, but the actual effects start one or two years after the DOE. Since there are no measured effects in the first full year, these provisions are considered to have zero effect, which may understate some budget impacts. Additionally, for the provision effective from months beginning after 12/31/18 in the document of Tax Cuts And Jobs Act, 10 2019 5 Document name: Estimated Budget Effects Of Division Q Of Amendment #2 To The Senate Amendment To H.R. 2029 (Rules Committee Print 114-40), The "Protecting Americans From Tax Hikes Act Of 2015" 6 Document name: Estimated Budget Effects Of The Conference Agreement For H.R. 4520, The "American Jobs Creation Act Of 2004" 7 "[30] Effective 180 days after the date on which the Secretary issues the regulations, which are required no later than 180 days after the date of enactment." 8 Document name: Estimated Budget Effects Of The Tax Provisions Contained In An Amendment In The Nature Of A Substitute To H.R. 1424, Scheduled For Consideration On The Senate Floor On October 1, 2008 9 Document name: Estimated Budget Effects Of Division P Of Amendment #1 To The Senate Amendment To H.R. 2029 (Rules Committee Print 114-39) 10 Document name: Estimated Budget Effects Of The Conference Agreement For H.R. 1, The "Tax Cuts And Jobs Act" is considered the first full year of effect, as the exact starting month in 2019 is unspecified.

p.s: Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT).
p.t: In the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, And Economic Security ('CARES') Act, 11 the first full year in effect of provisions with DOE as effective dates should be 2021 according to the rule stated above, assuming the publication date (April, 23, 2020) as the enactment date. However, reflecting the short-term nature of the legislation, some provisions report much bigger effects in the first year (2020) than in the second year, which is the first full year. Despite this, we strictly follow the rules, potentially downplaying the effects of this particular legislation with short-term impacts. In the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, 12 we assume the first year in effect as the budget effect year for provisions with effective dates referring to other legislation (e.g., "Effective as if included in section 2201 of CARES Act (Public Law 116-136)"). Generally, we consider the first five years of budget effects given in a table for each legislation. However, exceptions exist in three pieces of legislation. If no provision shows a full-year effect in the first year presented, we drop the first year and use the second year as the starting point for the five-year period. This can occur in two scenarios: A) no effect is measured in the first year despite it being the first full-cycle year, and B) some effect is measured in the first year of legislation, but the first year is not the first full-cycle year. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 can serve as an example for the first scenario. 13 The examples for the second scenario can also be observed in the Children's Health Insurance Program Reauthorization Act Of 2009 14 and Families First Coronavirus Response Act. 15 11
